one_liner: Rust crypto on formally verified s2n-bignum assembly, a rustls backend; one-handshake processes ran 1.6-3.8x faster than OpenSSL-backed.
what_it_does: Graviola provides the primitives that modern web TLS uses: X25519, P-256/P-384 ECDH, ML-KEM-768, ECDSA, Ed25519, RSA-PSS/PKCS#1 signing and verification, SHA-2/SHA-3, HMAC, and AES-GCM and (X)ChaCha20-Poly1305. The public Rust API is small and typed (for example `key_agreement::x25519::PrivateKey::new_random()`, `aead::AesGcm`, `signing::ecdsa::SigningKey`). The main use is the companion crate rustls-graviola: call `rustls_graviola::default_provider().install_default()` and rustls then runs on Graviola instead of ring or aws-lc-rs. It does not replace OpenSSL's C API or ABI; it replaces the crypto provider under a Rust TLS stack.
how_it_is_fast: The field and group arithmetic for P-256, P-384, X25519/Ed25519, the RSA bignums, the ML-KEM NTT and Keccak-f is AWS s2n-bignum's hand-written, formally verified assembly, which a script converts into Rust inline `asm!` so only rustc is needed. It uses Booth-encoded fixed windows for point multiplication (7-bit with a 148 KB precomputed table for the P-256 base point, 5-bit elsewhere) and a 4-bit fixed window with CRT for RSA. Other parts are tuned for specific CPU features: stitched by-8 AES-CTR plus by-8 GHASH, an optional AVX-512/VAES by-16 path chosen at runtime, SHA-NI and Arm SHA intrinsics, and 4-way AVX2 Keccak for ML-KEM sampling. In the handshake benchmark the lead over OpenSSL is a nearly constant 3.1-4.7 ms, which points to a fixed per-process cost on the OpenSSL side, not to faster handshake math.
when_to_use: Rust services on rustls 0.23 whose handshakes use ECDSA-P256, X25519 or X25519MLKEM768. Graviola's own benchmark ranks it first in ECDSA-P256 signing (92,694 vs aws-lc-rs 85,967 sigs/s on a Ryzen 9 7940HS), X25519 (42,363 vs 42,038 kx/s) and ML-KEM-768 (33,520 vs 31,044 per s).
Builds that must avoid a C compiler, CMake or assembler, such as cross-compiling or hermetic cargo-only CI. The README says the crate builds in under one second with only rustc.

Short-lived processes such as CLIs, test harnesses and serverless cold starts that do one TLS 1.3 handshake. In the c410-f3r test on a Ryzen 9 5900X, a whole run took about 1.3-5.9 ms with Graviola and 4.4-10.2 ms with the OpenSSL backend.
Arm hosts with AES, SHA2 and PMULL (Apple M-series, Raspberry Pi 5). Graviola leads on aarch64 in ECDSA-P256 signing (84,286 vs aws-lc-rs 64,224 sigs/s on an M2) and in ML-KEM-768.
Cases where formally verified bignum and ECC code, constant-time table selection, Arm DIT and SIMD-register zeroing after secret operations matter more than FIPS certification.
when_not_to_use: Servers that sign handshakes with RSA keys. On x86_64, RSA-2048 signing runs at 2,280.7 sigs/s against 5,276.3 for aws-lc-rs. Issue #209 traces this to bignum_emontredc_8n.

P-384 certificates or key exchange. Graviola reaches roughly 56-68% of aws-lc-rs throughput here (ECDSA-P384 signing 9,175.8 vs 16,385 sigs/s; P384 kx 4,861.2 vs 7,197 kx/s). In the handshake blog, aws-lc-rs also beat it with P-384 certificates.
Bulk AES-256-GCM throughput. Graviola ranks third on x86_64 (8.79 vs 9.88 GiB/s for aws-lc-rs) and fourth on the M2 (5.25 GiB/s).

CPUs without ADX, AVX2 or BMI2, including Haswell, VMs that hide ADX (issue #222: an OVH VPS reported as 'Haswell, no TSX') and Raspberry Pi 4. Also RISC-V, 32-bit, wasm and no_std targets. None of these have a software fallback (issues #95, #57).

Projects that need the OpenSSL API or C ABI, FIPS, an audited and mature library (the README says 'very new, so exercise due caution'), QUIC through quinn (still unmerged, issue #98), SHA-1, ML-DSA or RSA encryption (a stated non-goal).

integration.dependencies: cfg-if, getrandom 0.3 (graviola); rustls 0.23.18+ (rustls-graviola). No C toolchain.
integration.min_toolchain: Rust 1.89, edition 2024 (graviola 0.4.1 rust-version); rustls-graviola 0.4.0 declares 1.85 but pulls in graviola 0.4.x
integration.platforms: x86_64 with AES, PCLMULQDQ, AVX, AVX2, BMI1/BMI2, ADX (Broadwell / AMD Zen and later; AVX-512 AES-GCM path used when present); aarch64 with NEON, AES, PMULL, SHA2. Needs std.
integration.thread_safety: not documented (safe Rust API; the crate does not state Send/Sync guarantees)

gotchas: An unsupported CPU does not return an error. Every public entry point runs `verify_cpu_features()`, and that function calls `assert!`, so the process panics on the first crypto call ('graviola requires adx CPU support'). Test on the real deployment hardware or VM type.
Valgrind does not emulate ADX (KDE bug 494162). Set the `VALGRIND_BUG_494162` environment variable at compile time (read by `option_env!`) to run under Valgrind.
RSA key generation is not side-channel safe. ECDSA uses hedged RFC 6979 nonces (extra random input), so repeated signatures of the same message differ.
GitHub shows the license as NOASSERTION. The real license is 'Apache-2.0 OR ISC OR MIT-0' (per Cargo.toml and SPDX headers), which license scanners that expect MIT or Apache may flag.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Graviola when you already use rustls in Rust and want a cargo-only build with top ECDSA-P256, X25519 and ML-KEM speed. Pick AWS-LC when you need an OpenSSL-style C API, FIPS, or fast RSA and P-384. Pick ztls or picotls fusion when the bottleneck is record or AEAD throughput, not handshakes.
verified_claims_summary: A third-party blog by the wtx author used hyperfine (10 runs after 10 warmups) on a Ryzen 9 5900X running Fedora (kernel 7.0.11) to time whole processes, each decoding PEM files, doing one TLS 1.3 handshake over loopback in wtx 0.49, and exiting; Graviola took about 1.26-5.90 ms and the OpenSSL backend 4.41-10.20 ms (the `openssl` 0.10 crate against unvendored system OpenSSL, version and rustc version not stated), so OpenSSL was 1.6-3.8x slower across 45 cipher, group and certificate combinations. OpenSSL was slowest in every combination, but Graviola was fastest in only 16 of 45, and the author cannot explain the near-constant 3.1-4.7 ms gap.
status_note: The project is active: last commit 2026-08-24, graviola 0.4.1 on crates.io (about 282k downloads), no RustSec advisories. It is pre-1.0 and describes itself as very new, and it is permissively licensed, so it is easy to adopt as a rustls provider but not yet a conservative choice.
